newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Surge in UK borrowing boosts rate rise case.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Surge in UK borrowing boosts rate rise case.

text.p: British consumer credit surged by over a billion pounds again in December, official figures said on Thursday, adding more weight to the central bank's case that interest rates will need to rise to keep inflation in check.

The Bank of England said consumer credit grew by 1.022 billion pounds ($1.6 billion) in December compared with 1.050 billion in November. Lending has grown by over a billion pounds in five out of the last six months.
The government welcomed the figures as proof consumers were enjoying more confidence, and it shrugged off suggestions that borrowing was starting to get out of control.

"In every region of Britain, consumers are more confident than they were a year ago. This confidence is showing in higher but sensible personal borrowing," said Michael Jack, financial secretary to the Treasury.

But City analysts said the figures will almost certainly ring alarm bells at the Bank of England and will strengthen Governor Eddie George's case for an immediate rate rise at next week's monetary meeting.

"The data will certainly support George's case for a rate rise at next week's meeting," said Mark Miller, UK economist at Morgan Stanley International. "Annual growth in borrowing is now running at over 16.5 percent, a six year high."
However, the borrowing figures are at odds with other recent data which suggested domestic demand was starting to slow of its own accord.

Official retail sales data for December showed high street activity slowed dramatically in the crucial pre-Christmas period with sales falling by 0.8 percent. Business surveys also said retailers were very disappointed by December business.
But the high rate of borrowing suggests consumers feel confident enough about future earnings to take on more debt.

"The trend remains firm enough to suggest the consumer sector is in good shape and willing to borrow more," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at Bank America. "This bodes well for a bounce back in spending this quarter."
Recent tax cuts and a modest rise in pay settlements mean take home pay has grown.
On top of this, a flood of windfall payments from building societies which plan to convert to banks later this year will leave consumers around 17 billion pounds better off.
The return of consumer confidence is good news for the government which must hold an election by May.
But the ruling Conservatives still trail opposition Labour by 20 points in the opinion polls and are likely to strongly oppose calls for a rate rise so close to polling day.

The credit figures come only a day after minutes from the monetary meeting in December revealed George warned Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke that failure to raise rates immediately by a quarter point would mean a half-point rise in January or February.
Clarke overruled George and kept rates on hold at 6.0 percent, saying the case had not been made for a further rise.
Economists said the Chancellor will probably oppose George's call for a rate rise on Wednesday too.
The Bank of England also released figures on Thursday showing mortgage approvals granted by banks and building societies eased to 6.1 billion pounds in December from 6.4 billion in November.

Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets, said the figures showed demand for mortgages was easing in response to rises in mortgage rates and uncertainty over further rises in the run up to the election.
"But the weakening suggests that consumer worries over higher interest rates will prevent a full-blown house price boom of the type seen in the late 1980s," he said.
